summary: Defines the Application-Layer Traffic Optimization protocol, which lets ISPs share simplified network maps and cost information with applications so they can choose better endpoints. It is aimed at peer-to-peer and content delivery uses.

plainLanguage.summary: An app that can download from many places can ask the network which is closest or cheapest. The network gives a simple map to help it pick well.

subtitle: A JSON-over-HTTP protocol that lets networks tell applications which endpoints are preferable to talk to.

tldr.problem: Applications that can choose between many endpoints, such as peer-to-peer systems and content delivery networks, cannot see what a provider prefers in terms of traffic, because that network information is hidden from the application layer.
tldr.mechanism: An ALTO server publishes simplified network maps that group endpoints into PIDs, cost maps between those PIDs, and endpoint property and endpoint cost lookups, all as JSON over HTTP discovered through an information resource directory.
tldr.outcome: Applications can pick better endpoints, and the network can steer load away from expensive links, while the provider can hide real values behind scores or rankings. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 9274.

today: RFC 7285 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 9274, so check that RFC for changes to this specification. The RFC itself says that discovery of the ALTO server is out of scope and that extensions may define further services, address types and error codes.

sections.title: The Problem ALTO Solves
sections.content:
Network details such as topologies, link availability, routing policies and path costs are hidden from the application layer, and many applications benefited from that. But new applications, such as application-layer overlays, can be adaptive and gain from knowing about the underlying network. The ALTO Protocol is an information-publishing interface through which a network publishes network locations, costs between them at configurable granularities, and endhost properties. It provides a solution for the problem stated in RFC 5693.

The benefit runs both ways. A network can better manage traffic on expensive or hard-to-provision links such as long-distance, transit or backup links, and it can protect sensitive state by abstracting real metric values into non-real numerical scores or ordinal rankings. An application can avoid bottlenecks, for example by not selecting peers behind high-delay links.

The design is REST-ful, encodes requests and responses in JSON, and reuses existing HTTP implementations, infrastructure and deployment experience.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally an app has no idea which of many friends lives closest. ALTO lets the network whisper hints, like which friend is on your street, so the app picks smartly.

sections.title: Servers, Clients and the My-Internet View
sections.content:
Each network region, which may be an AS, an ISP, a smaller region or a set of ISPs, can provide ALTO services that describe the Internet from its own perspective. The RFC calls this the my-Internet view. It does not expose internal topology, so it is a "single-node" abstract topology.

An ALTO server prepares the information, an ALTO client uses ALTO service discovery to find an appropriate server, and the client then requests information using the ALTO Protocol. The server may draw on routing protocols, provisioning policy, dynamic network information and outside parties, but those parts are outside the scope of the RFC. The information can be updated dynamically or be treated as a policy updated on a longer time scale. ALTO may convey dynamic information, but it is not intended to replace near-real-time congestion control protocols.

Because ALTO is HTTP-based, it can integrate with the existing HTTP caching infrastructure, so a response may come from a third party. Expiration times and digital signatures for returned information are left for future investigation.
sections.plainLanguage: Each neighborhood draws its own map of the world from where it sits. The app asks the neighborhood's map-keeper for hints, and the keeper never has to show every pipe and wire.

sections.title: Network Maps, PIDs and Cost Maps
sections.content:
Many endpoints are near one another in network terms, so an ALTO server groups them. Each group is a Provider-defined Identifier (PID): a name plus the set of endpoint addresses it covers. A PID may denote a subnet, a metropolitan area, a point of presence or an autonomous system, whichever granularity the provider chooses. A network map lists every PID and its addresses.

A cost map gives the path cost for pairs of PIDs. Cost is directional, from source to destination. Network maps and cost maps can be updated on different time scales, so each cost map carries the version tag of the network map it was built from. A version tag is a resource ID plus an opaque tag string, and whenever a network map changes, its tag MUST change.

A cost has a metric (what it measures) and a mode (how to read it). Servers MUST offer the routingcost metric, where a lower value means a higher preference. A server MUST support at least one of the two modes: numerical, where arithmetic such as ratios for load balancing is safe, and ordinal, where values are only a ranking and need not be unique or contiguous.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of listing every house, the map puts nearby houses into neighborhoods with names. Then a second sheet says how far each neighborhood is from every other one.

sections.title: Mapping IP Addresses to PIDs
sections.content:
For maps that use the ipv4 and ipv6 address types, clients and servers MUST use longest-prefix matching to turn an IP address into a PID. To make that give exactly one answer, the map must have two properties.

  • Complete: every possible address is covered. A recommended way is to include 0.0.0.0/0 for IPv4 and ::/0 for IPv6 in some PID.
  • Non-overlapping: no two PIDs may contain an identical IP prefix.

The RFC shows that merging two adjacent prefixes in one PID into a single prefix that matches another PID's prefix would make the map overlapping, so an address like 192.0.2.1 could no longer be mapped unambiguously. Extension documents may allow one address to map to multiple PIDs.
sections.plainLanguage: To find which neighborhood your house is in, you pick the smallest labeled area that contains it. Every house must fit in at least one area, and no two areas may claim exactly the same patch.

sections.title: The Four ALTO Services
sections.content:
ALTO groups its functions into information services that a client can request individually.

  • The Map Service serves the whole network map and cost maps as batch information, which the RFC says can be implemented as simple files.
  • The Map-Filtering Service lets a resource-constrained client ask for a subset, by POSTing a list of PIDs or address types, or source and destination PIDs and cost constraints. Constraints use operators gt, lt, ge, le and eq. A server may or may not provide it.
  • The Endpoint Property Service looks up properties of individual endpoints. A server MUST define the pid property for each network map it provides.
  • The Endpoint Cost Service returns costs, or rankings, directly among endpoints. If a source or destination list is empty, the server uses the address the client connected from, and the two lists MUST NOT both be empty.

Additional services can be defined in companion documents.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four counters at the help desk: one hands out the whole map, one hands out just the part you ask for, one tells you facts about a single address, and one ranks addresses for you.

sections.title: HTTP, Directories and Errors
sections.content:
Every ALTO exchange is ordinary HTTP. Each information resource has its own JSON media type, such as application/alto-networkmap+json and application/alto-costmap+json, rather than plain application/json. Resources without input parameters use GET. Resources with parameters use POST with a body of the matching parameters media type, and a client MUST NOT assume GET and POST are interchangeable.

A client starts from its Root Information Resource Directory (IRD), a JSON document that lists each resource with its uri, media-type, and optional accepts, capabilities and uses attributes. The Root IRD MUST name a default-alto-network-map. An IRD entry can point to another IRD, which lets a server delegate resources to another domain.

Responses have a meta field and, where needed, a data component. Errors are returned as application/alto-error+json with a code in meta: E_SYNTAX, E_MISSING_FIELD, E_INVALID_FIELD_TYPE or E_INVALID_FIELD_VALUE. A server MUST also set a proper HTTP status code. When overloaded it SHOULD return 503 or 307, and clients MUST ignore unknown fields. Implementations MUST support HTTPS and TLS, and where client authentication is wanted, HTTP Digest Authentication MUST be supported, with TLS client authentication preferred if available.
sections.plainLanguage: Asking ALTO a question is just like opening a web page. A table of contents tells you which page has which kind of answer, and if you ask wrongly you get a note saying what was wrong.

sections.title: Use Cases: Peer-to-Peer Applications
sections.content:
The RFC's use cases focus on peer-to-peer applications, and note that ALTO can also apply to environments such as content distribution networks. In the first, a P2P tracker acts as an ALTO client. It fetches the network map and the cost map from the ISP's ALTO server, then builds a peer list for each joining client based on those maps and possibly other sources. It could even use only the network map to prefer peers in the same PID and ISP.

In the second, a P2P client fetches the maps itself, typically from its own ISP's ALTO server, and uses the numerical costs as part of its peer selection algorithm. In the third, the client collects candidate peers from sources such as peer exchange, DHTs and trackers, then asks the Endpoint Cost Service to rank them using the ordinal cost mode, and connects in that order. The RFC limits this third case to when the P2P client and ALTO server are deployed by the same entity.
sections.plainLanguage: A file-sharing app asks the network which other users are nearby and cheap to reach, then connects to those first.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Risks
sections.content:
The RFC treats several threats. A forged cost map or directory could, for example, turn a distributed application into a DDoS tool by strongly preferring one small address range. ALTO relies on the authenticity and integrity mechanisms of HTTP over TLS to protect against this.

Even authentic guidance can be bad. A provider hostile to some applications could misuse cost maps, and if many clients follow guidance blindly, preferred hosts could be overloaded. There is no protocol mechanism that forces how applications use ALTO information, so an application may check whether results beat random choice and disable ALTO or switch to an independent server.

Maps can also leak topology and policy, so providers should judge how much detail to reveal and may require client authentication. For user privacy, clients can avoid cookies, use only PIDs rather than IP addresses where possible, or send shorter prefixes, at some cost in accuracy. For availability, queries with n sources and m destinations make the server compute n*m path costs, so access control, overload rejection and pre-generated maps are suggested.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone gives the app fake hints, it could send everyone to the wrong place. So the app should check the hints really came from the network, and not tell the keeper more about itself than needed.
